summary: L-lysine is an essential amino acid that must be obtained from the diet (e.g., meat, dairy, legumes). It is marketed as an over-the-counter nutritional supplement, generally recognized as safe at typical doses, and is popularly used - on the basis of limited and mixed evidence - to reduce the frequency or severity of recurrent herpes labialis (cold sores). Typical oral supplemental doses are around 1000 mg, with total intake commonly in the range of 1-3 g/day. It is a dietary supplement rather than an FDA-approved drug; very high doses may cause gastrointestinal upset such as diarrhea and abdominal cramps.

moa: L-lysine is one of the essential amino acids required for protein synthesis and normal growth; it is a building block for body proteins and a precursor for carnitine synthesis. The body cannot synthesize lysine, so it must come from the diet or supplements. The popular use for cold sores is theorized to relate to lysine competing with the amino acid arginine, which herpes simplex virus uses for replication; however, the clinical evidence supporting this benefit is limited and inconsistent.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to L-lysine or product excipients
relative: Significant renal impairment (use caution; consult a clinician)
Lysinuric protein intolerance or other inborn errors of lysine metabolism

preg: Lysine is an essential amino acid normally obtained from the diet and present in the body. Specific safety data for high-dose supplementation in pregnancy are limited; pregnant individuals should obtain lysine through a balanced diet and consult a clinician before taking supplements.
lact: Lysine is a normal dietary constituent and is present in breast milk as part of normal protein content. Data on high-dose supplementation during breastfeeding are limited; obtain through normal diet and consult a clinician before using supplements.
renal: There is no established dose adjustment for the supplement, but caution is advised in significant renal impairment. People with kidney disease should consult a clinician before taking amino acid supplements.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is described for the supplement. Use the usual precautions and consult a clinician if significant liver disease is present.

moderate: Calcium supplements (lysine may increase calcium absorption and reduce its excretion - theoretical effect)
minor: Arginine-rich supplements (theoretical competition with lysine; relevant to the cold-sore rationale)

pearls: L-lysine is a dietary supplement (OTC), not an FDA-approved drug; it is generally recognized as safe at typical intakes
Use for preventing recurrent cold sores (herpes labialis) is popular but supported only by limited and mixed evidence
The proposed cold-sore mechanism is competition with arginine, which herpes simplex virus needs to replicate - this remains unproven
Very high doses can cause gastrointestinal upset such as diarrhea and abdominal cramps
missed: Because this is a nutritional supplement, a missed dose is not harmful. Take it when remembered, or simply resume the usual schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Lysine has a wide margin of safety. Excessive intake is most likely to cause gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea and abdominal cramps. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive (stop the supplement, maintain hydration). Seek medical advice if symptoms are severe or persistent.
